ephemeris: Mercury 13 Nov 07:55 PST, Venus 13 Nov 16:32 PST.

claim: Mars–Jupiter conjunction exact on 14 November, in Leo near Regulus
ephemeris: Exact in longitude 2026-11-16 06:24 UTC at 25.5° Leo. On 24 November Mars is 1.8° and Jupiter 3.7° from Regulus.

claim: Full Moon on 24 November at 6:54 a.m. PST
It is a supermoon (Moon near its closest)
ephemeris: Perigee 25 Nov 12:54 PST at 359,347 km; at full Moon 360,765 km. The Moon's tidal pull is about 20% above its average, the total spring tide about 15% higher; West Coast king tides are expected around this date in any case.

claim: The last double retrograde (March 2025) brought the M7.7 Myanmar earthquake
ephemeris: Myanmar struck on 28 March 2025 with both planets retrograde. Over 1965–2016, days with both retrograde had 5 M7+ mainshocks against 7.2 expected by chance (alignment test below).

claim: Uranus opposition on 25 November, Moon conjunct Uranus at full Moon
ephemeris: Opposition 2026-11-25 22:24 UTC; Moon–Uranus conjunction 24 Nov 09:05 PST; 1.4° apart in longitude at the full Moon.

claim: Uranus–Neptune–Pluto 'minor grand trine' (two sextiles and a trine)
ephemeris: At the full Moon: Uranus–Neptune 62.0°, Neptune–Pluto 58.3°, Uranus–Pluto 120.3° (exact would be 60°, 60°, 120°). These slow angles last for years.

claim: At Frazier Park, Sun rising and Moon setting at the full Moon, Mars and Jupiter overhead
ephemeris: At 06:54 PST: Sun +2.0°, Moon -0.7° altitude; Mars 64° up (azimuth 218°), Jupiter 62° up. Sunrise 06:38, moonset 06:54 PST. The same Sun-up/Moon-down geometry happens somewhere along the dawn line at every full Moon.

claim: Planetary tides are about 1/150 of the Moon's
ephemeris: Venus, the strongest, raises a tide about 1/20,000 of the Moon's even at its closest; all planets together are far below 1/150.

claim: Alignments, supermoons and double retrogrades raise the chance of a great earthquake
ephemeris: No excess of M6+, M7+ or M7.5+ mainshocks in 1965–2016 around these configurations (tests on this tab). Tidal triggering is real but small (Ide et al. 2016): far too weak to forecast a particular quake.

claim: A record El Niño and coastal Kelvin wave add seismic energy to California
ephemeris: A sea-level rise of 20–30 cm loads the crust by about 0.02–0.03 bar, less than the ordinary daily ocean tide; no link between ENSO and large earthquakes is established.
